name: lentil potato stew
instructions:
A french/italian lentil-and-potato stew built on pureed portabella mushrooms + finely chopped potatoes + lentils. The potato-and-pureed-mushroom base carries the dish — they fill the 'meat' slot together (see notes on why this makes the base amenable to either french or italian seasoning without committing to either cuisine specifically).

AXIS OF VARIATION: tomato-forward or stock-forward. Same recipe body; the ratio of tomato-and-tomato-paste to stock is what shifts the register.

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. SOFFRITO: sauté finely chopped yellow onion, celery, and carrots in olive oil until softened.
2. PUREED PORTABELLAS: puree the portabella mushrooms in a food processor or blender, then add to the pot. Cook them down into the soffrito base — they should reduce and deepen in color.
3. TOMATO STEP: add finely chopped fresh tomato (half or one whole for stock-forward; up to 1-2 whole for tomato-forward — see notes). If going tomato-forward, add a spoonful of tomato paste and cook it hard into the oil until it darkens a shade.
4. HERBS + SEASONING: add bay leaf (kept in and fished out later) and your herb mix — see herbs note. Any combination of rosemary (used lightly), herbes de provence, and dried oregano works. Season with black pepper and salt.
5. POTATOES + LENTILS: fold in finely chopped potatoes (small dice — see notes) and lentils. Both go in at the same time so they cook at the same rate.
6. STOCK: pour in stock — how much depends on tomato-vs-stock balance (see notes). Less stock reads more tomato-concentrated / italian-ragu-adjacent; more stock reads brothier / french-provincial-adjacent.
7. SLOW COOK covered for a long time.
8. If the broth is thinner than you want at the end, stir in a small starch slurry to finish.
notes:
=== NAMED 'LENTIL POTATO STEW' NOT 'LENTIL MUSHROOM STEW' ===

Renamed because the potatoes are the more accurate structural headline. Mushrooms are pureed and dissolve into the broth as a meat-slot backbone; the potatoes are the visible starchy body every spoonful gets. The old 'lentil mushroom stew' name over-emphasized the mushroom role.

=== WHY THIS BASE WORKS — POTATOES + PUREED MUSHROOMS ARE THE 'MEAT' ===

The pureed mushrooms + finely chopped potatoes fill the 'meat' slot together. In a bolognese or lentil chili, the meat is the meat; here, the mushroom-and-potato combo carries the protein-and-body role. Because that role isn't itself french or italian, the same base takes seasonings from either cuisine without committing to one — that's why the recipe is tagged both. This is what distinguishes lentil potato stew from italian minestrone (which is committed to the italian tomato path) and from french chicken soup (which is committed to the wine-and-herb path).

=== AXIS OF VARIATION — TOMATO-FORWARD OR STOCK-FORWARD ===

The recipe has one real variation axis: how much of the broth is tomato vs stock. It's a continuous dial, not a hard fork:

- TOMATO-FORWARD END: 1-2 whole tomatoes finely chopped + a spoonful of tomato paste cooked hard into the oil until darkened + minimum stock (just enough for coverage). Reads dense and italian-ragu-adjacent. The dish concentrates on the tomato-and-mushroom-and-potato combination.
- STOCK-FORWARD END: half or one whole tomato (light, structural — no tomato paste) + generous stock. Reads brothier and closer to a proper french provincial vegetable stew.

Either end works; mid-range works too. Pick based on the day's mood. The seasoning stays the same across both ends — the same herb mix (rosemary, herbes de provence, bay leaf, oregano — mix as desired) works on either end of the axis.

=== POTATOES ARE NON-OPTIONAL — FINELY CHOPPED, ADDED WITH THE LENTILS ===

Potatoes are load-bearing, not an optional add-on. Chop them FINELY (small dice — not large chunks) so they cook at roughly the same rate as the lentils, and add them at the same time. The potatoes contribute two things the dish needs: (1) starchy body that thickens the broth structurally as it simmers, replacing much of the need for the starch slurry finish, and (2) a starchy carb texture in each bite that softens the otherwise-monolithic lentil-and-mushroom mouthfeel. Without potatoes the stew reads thin and one-textured. Finely chopping — not chunk-cutting — matters because you want the potato distributed through every spoonful.

=== PUREED MUSHROOMS — NOT CHOPPED ===

Portabella mushrooms should be pureed (food processor or blender) before adding, then cooked down into the base. Pureeing gives them a dense meaty backbone that reads as protein-and-body rather than as visible mushroom pieces. This matches the potato-as-carb move — both structural ingredients dissolve into the broth and support it structurally rather than showing up as discrete chunks. Chopped mushrooms give you a different (chunkier, less integrated) dish.

=== HERBS — ROSEMARY, HERBES DE PROVENCE, BAY LEAF, OREGANO (MIX AS DESIRED) ===

All four work together, and you can lean toward whichever combination matches your mood. Rosemary provides the piney second dimension against the mushroom-and-lentil base — use it lightly, since at full quantity it dominates. Herbes de provence rounds the herb axis with sage/lavender/thyme-in-the-mix character; use it more generously. Bay leaf sits quietly in the simmer adding depth without pushing a direction — whole leaves in, fished out before serving. Oregano is the italian baseline — reliable and doesn't fight the others. Fennel seeds (crushed in a mortar) or fennel powder add a ratatouille-adjacent lean if you want it — optional.

Don't reach for basil or parsley here — they're finishing herbs for other italian dishes, not simmer herbs for a stew.

=== NO WINE — DOESN'T DO MUCH FOR THIS DISH ===

White wine used to be primary in the french variant of this recipe. Removed and moved to clashing. On repeated testing, the wine doesn't do much for the finished dish — the mushroom + potato + lentil base is dense enough that the wine's acid and depth get absorbed rather than lifting anything. Save the white wine for dishes where it does structural work (chicken-with-vinegar, coq-au-vin, french-chicken-soup, lemony-shrimp-and-bean-stew). Here, more stock or a spoonful more tomato paste does the flavor-building job more effectively.

=== NO THYME, NO OLD BAY, NO CANNED TOMATOES ===

- THYME: inappropriate here. The dish is mushroom-and-lentil dominant — a relatively monolithic savory profile — so it wants rosemary + herbes de provence + oregano rather than thyme. Herbes de provence contains a little thyme in its blend, which is fine, but standalone dried thyme is wrong. See the herbs and greens article on the thyme-vs-rosemary axis.
- OLD BAY: belongs in italian-minestrone-soup-shaped dishes that explicitly choose it. This dish has its own herb backbone; old bay would fight it.
- CANNED TOMATOES: push the dish toward a wrong tomato register. Use fresh tomatoes (finely chopped) plus optional tomato paste — canned reads too soupy and washed-out here.

=== STOCK IS PRIMARY — NOT BOUILLON CUBES ===

This dish wants a real stock as the liquid, not bouillon cubes. The mushroom-and-lentil profile benefits from stock's gentler, more layered body — bouillon cubes are too concentrated and salty. Vegetable stock is the reliable default; beef stock or chicken stock could work but change the register.

=== STARCH SLURRY FINISH — OPTIONAL ===

If the broth ends up thinner than you want, stir in a small starch slurry at the end. Not always needed — the pureed mushrooms, potatoes, and lentils usually carry enough body — but it's the right move when the stew is too brothy.

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- lentil-wellington: same lentil + mushroom umami DNA, but in a baked-log format wrapped in puff pastry. If you like the flavor of this stew but want a fancier presentation, that's the destination.
- italian-minestrone-soup: the committed-italian-tomato-path cousin. Different structural logic (broth-forward, more vegetables); reach for that when you want a proper italian minestrone rather than the flexible stew here.
- french-chicken-soup: the committed-french-wine-and-herb-path cousin (with chicken as the protein). Different protein, different broth register.
